newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador's Bucaram seen losing hold on power.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador's Bucaram seen losing hold on power.

text.p: Embattled President Abdala Bucaram of Ecuador appeared to be losing his shaky hold on power on Saturday amid reports that the military had withdrawn all support for his 6-month-old government.

Bucaram, who left the heavy fortified presidential palace in Quito late on Friday for his traditional power base in Guayaquil, has dismissed Thursday's vote by Congress deposing him on grounds of mental incompetence as an attempted coup and said he had no intention of stepping down.

But national radio said he had lost all support from the military, which handed over power to a civilian government in 1979 but remains a powerful behind-the-scenes player in the political life of this South American country.
"Bucaram no longer has the support of the military high command," Radio Quito said in a news bulletin, citing what it said were sources close to senior military officials.

"Bucaram will no longer receive military honours corresponding to the rank of chief of state and his armed guard will be limited, as is only understandable, to the security detail a former head of state is entitled to," it added.

The report could not be immediately confirmed. But defence ministry sources said the military high command was preparing to issue a communique later on Saturday about the political crisis that has seen three top politicians vying for Ecuador's top job since Thursday night.
Vice President Rosalia Arteaga and congressional leader Fabian Alarcon have both staked claims to the presidency in the aftermath of Bucaram's summary dismissal by Congress.

The military has vowed to maintain a neutral stance in the conflict, and has stopped short so far of backing either Alarcon, Arteaga or Bucaram, in public. But many analysts see it as playing a crucial role in choosing Bucaram's possible successor and ending the deepening constitutional conflict.

Bucaram -- who served as mayor of Guayaquil in the 1980s before corruption charges forced him to flee to Panama -- staged what looked like a triumphant return to the city late on Friday after abandoning the ornate Carondelet presidential palace for the first time since Thursday night's vote.

At an impromptu news conference, the populist candidate, who won a solid victory in most of Ecuador's 21 provinces before taking office just six months ago, said democracy would cease to exist without him.

"Abdala represents democracy, anything else would be a coup," he said. He also challenged Alarcon to demonstrate his "manhood" by meeting him in Guayaquil late on Saturday to thrash out their political differences face-to-face.

Alarcon, who led thousands of supporters in an aborted attempt to storm the presidential palace on Friday, responded to the challenge by likening Bucaram to a punchy and "foul-mouthed" boxer looking to slug it out in a ring that was crumbling beneath him.
"This isn't a question of boxers having to climb into the ring (with him)," Alarcon said. He dismissed any chance of a meeting with Bucaram or talks aimed at ironing out their differences in private.

An 18-year-old student was killed and at least six other people were injured as Alarcon's supporters clashed with riot police near the Carondelet presidential palace on Friday and Alarcon subsequently announced that he was beginning an indefinite hunger strike to force Bucaram to hand over power.

In its lead editorial on Saturday, Quito's respected El Comercio newspaper urged all three pretenders to the presidential throne to step aside in favour of someone else. The alternative, it warned, would only be a further escalation of the constitutional conflict, which threatens to erupt in serious political bloodetting.

The conservative daily said there was no doubt about the "constitutional origin" of Bucaram's mandate. But amid allegations of corruption and nepotism, and the many errors he has committed over the past six months, Bucaram has been weakend too severely to rule, it said.

It added that Alarcon's election by Congress was clouded in controversy and stressed that while Arteaga appeared to be Bucaram's legitimate heir, she lacked the grassroots support needed to lead the country out of its deepening crisis.
